issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette: John, a 60-year-old European American male and a warehouse worker, has been struggling with profound distress since his military service ended years ago. Despite the passage of time, John’s traumatic experiences continue to haunt him on multiple levels, deeply impacting his daily life and relationships. The trauma occurred during his deployment in Afghanistan, where he was part of a mission that went terribly wrong. His unit came under intense enemy fire while they were conducting a patrol near a small village. The chaos and confusion were overwhelming as explosions erupted around them, and the acrid smell of smoke filled the air. John had to take cover behind a makeshift barrier while his comrades fought valiantly beside him. In that moment of sheer terror, he saw several fellow soldiers fall, their bodies twisted in pain and death. The sound of gunfire and screams echoed through his ears as he tried desperately to protect himself and those around him. The trauma has left John with intense guilt and a deep sense of loss. He avoids going near the areas where the event took place, even the mere thought of being close to such locations is unbearable. Similarly, he refuses to wear clothes that remind him of his time in service, as it triggers memories of that fateful day. The act of thinking about the event itself is almost too much for John; he avoids it at all costs because it brings back a flood of emotions and vivid details that are overwhelming. When John does recall the incident, he feels intense guilt and terror. He knows exactly what happened, but finding words to describe it is nearly impossible, as if his language has been rendered inadequate by the sheer magnitude of the event. The memory is so potent that it brings back the same visceral fear he felt at the time, making him relive the horror repeatedly. John’s internal world has become a place of constant doubt and pain. He feels guilty for surviving when others did not, questioning his worthiness to be alive in light of what happened. This survival guilt has led him to feel like he doesn’t know himself anymore—a shadow of who he once was before the trauma. The event has also made him believe that the world is inherently dangerous, a perspective that colors every aspect of his life. In his occupation as a warehouse worker, John’s avoidance behaviors have manifested in ways that affect his daily functioning and relationships with coworkers. He avoids areas within the warehouse that remind him of the locations he had to navigate during combat. This has led to misunderstandings and decreased productivity at work, as he often delays tasks or takes circuitous routes around certain sections. His relationship with his partner has also been strained by these avoidance behaviors and intense emotions. John’s reluctance to discuss what happened in the military frustrates his partner, who feels left out of a significant part of John’s life. The guilt and terror associated with memories make it difficult for him to engage fully in their relationship or participate in activities they used to enjoy together. Despite his efforts to avoid triggers and keep his memories at bay, John has reached a point where the distress is too much to bear alone. He finally decided to seek help after experiencing a particularly intense episode of guilt and fear that left him feeling overwhelmed and isolated. What frightens him most now is the prospect of living with these feelings indefinitely without relief. However, he also hopes for a chance to regain some sense of normalcy and peace in his life. In therapy, John’s journey will involve addressing both his maladaptive strategies and the negative appraisals that have taken root since his traumatic experience. Through this process, he aims to find ways to manage his symptoms and reclaim aspects of himself that were lost during those harrowing moments in Afghanistan.
